content: Vitamin K refers to a group of fat-soluble vitamins that are essential for the post-translational modification of specific proteins, primarily those involved in blood coagulation. Chemically, these vitamins are derivatives of 2-methyl-1,4-naphthoquinone. Vitamin K2 (menaquinone or menatetrenone) is typically synthesized by intestinal bacteria, and dietary deficiency is rare unless there is significant intestinal damage. Vitamin K is a collective term for compounds that share a methylated naphthoquinone ring structure but differ in the aliphatic side chain attached at the 3-position. Phylloquinone (Vitamin K1) has a side chain with four isoprenoid residues, one of which is unsaturated. Menaquinones, on the other hand, have variable numbers of unsaturated isoprenoid residues and are designated as MK-n, where n indicates the number of isoprenoids. The naphthoquinone group is the functional component, and the mechanism of action is consistent across all K vitamins. However, differences in intestinal absorption, transport, tissue distribution, and bioavailability arise due to variations in the lipophilicity of the side chains and the food matrices in which they are found. Vitamin K plays a critical role in the carboxylation of specific glutamate residues in proteins, converting them into gamma-carboxyglutamate (Gla) residues. These Gla residues are essential for calcium binding and are crucial for the biological activity of all known Gla-proteins. To date, 14 human Gla-proteins have been identified, and they are involved in regulating blood coagulation, bone metabolism, and vascular biology. Blood Coagulation Vitamin K is integral to blood coagulation by activating both coagulation and anticoagulation pathways. It facilitates the gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues in prothrombin (Factor II), Factors VII, IX, X, Protein C, Protein S, and Protein Z. The enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase converts vitamin K into its active form, enabling these processes. Bone Metabolism Vitamin K contributes to bone mineralization by carboxylating vitamin K-dependent proteins such as osteocalcin, synthesized by osteoblasts, and matrix Gla protein (MGP), found in cartilage. It regulates calcium balance by influencing the synthesis and excretion of nephrocalcin and interleukins 1 and 6. High doses of vitamin K2 and low doses of vitamin K1 have been shown to increase bone density in osteoporosis and reduce fracture rates. Its effects on bone health are synergistic with vitamin D. Vascular Biology Matrix Gla protein (MGP), present in cartilage and blood vessels, prevents atherosclerosis and reduces age-related arterial stiffness. The recommended dietary intake (RDI) for a 25-year-old male is 120 micrograms per day, with no established tolerable upper intake level (UL). The body stores vitamin K, so daily intake is not mandatory. Sources of Vitamin K Vitamin K is abundant in leafy green vegetables (e.g., spinach, lettuce), Brassica vegetables (e.g., kale, cabbage, broccoli), wheat bran, organ meats, cereals, certain fruits (e.g., avocado, kiwi, bananas), meats, dairy products, eggs, and soy products. Phylloquinone (Vitamin K1) is the primary dietary form and is found in chicken egg yolk, butter, cow liver, most cheeses, and some mayonnaise types. Two tablespoons of parsley provide 153% of the recommended daily amount of vitamin K. Vitamin K Deficiency Deficiency can result from poor dietary intake (e.g., malnutrition, starvation, fasting, post-chemotherapy anorexia, total parenteral nutrition), malabsorption (e.g., celiac disease), or antibiotic use. It may also occur due to impaired intestinal uptake (e.g., bile duct obstruction), ingestion of vitamin K antagonists, or, rarely, nutritional deficiency. Deficiency leads to incomplete formation of Gla residues, rendering Gla-proteins inactive. This can result in uncontrolled internal bleeding, cartilage calcification, severe bone malformation, or deposition of insoluble calcium salts in arterial walls. Indications for Vitamin K Warfarin Overdose Vitamin K administration can mitigate bleeding risks in patients with warfarin over-anticoagulation. Oral and intravenous routes are more effective than subcutaneous administration, with oral routes preferred due to ease of use and absence of anaphylaxis. Superwarfarin Toxicity Superwarfarins, long-acting rodenticides, are 100 times more potent than warfarin. Examples include brodifacoum, bromadiolone, coumafuryl, and difenacoum. Poisoning risks arise from occupational hazards, drug abuse, accidental exposure, or suicide attempts. Diagnosis involves superwarfarin assays and abnormal coagulation profiles (elevated PT, aPTT, INR). Treatment requires high doses of vitamin K for extended periods (weeks to months). Use in Newborns In some countries, vitamin K injections are routinely administered to newborns to prevent late-onset hemorrhagic disease (HDN). However, HDN is rare, and some parents opt out of this prophylactic measure. Biochemistry and Discovery In the late 1920s, Henrik Dam discovered vitamin K while studying cholesterol in chickens fed a cholesterol-depleted diet. The animals developed hemorrhages that could not be reversed by adding purified cholesterol, leading to the identification of a coagulation vitamin. The vitamin was named K after the German word Koagulationsvitamin. Edward Doisy elucidated its structure and chemical nature, and both scientists shared the 1943 Nobel Prize in Medicine. Early quantification of vitamin K relied on a chick model, where vitamin K-deficient chicks were fed known amounts of vitamin K-containing food, and coagulation restoration was measured. Vitamin K undergoes electron reduction to its active form, vitamin K hydroquinone, via the enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKOR). This hydroquinone is oxidized during the carboxylation of glutamate to Gla by gamma-glutamyl carboxylase. The carboxylation and epoxidation reactions are coupled, and vitamin K epoxide is recycled back to vitamin K by VKOR. This recycling process explains why vitamin K deficiency is rare. Warfarin and other coumarin drugs inhibit VKOR, reducing tissue concentrations of vitamin K and its hydroquinone form, impairing Gla formation. This results in clotting factors with diminished or absent Gla residues, preventing stable binding to blood vessel endothelium and clot formation during injury. Warfarin administration requires careful monitoring to avoid overdosing. Gla-Proteins Human Gla-containing proteins include blood coagulation factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX, X, anticoagulant proteins C and S, and Factor X-targeting protein Z. Bone Gla-protein osteocalcin, calcification-inhibiting matrix Gla protein (MGP), and growth arrest-specific gene 6 protein (Gas6) are also Gla-proteins. Gas6 functions as a growth factor, activating the Axl receptor tyrosine kinase to stimulate cell proliferation or prevent apoptosis. Gla residues are essential for the functional activity of these proteins, which are found in mammals, birds, reptiles, and fish. Some Australian snake venoms contain Gla-containing enzymes that activate human blood clotting, leading to potentially fatal clotting. Fish-hunting snails like Conus geographus produce venom with neuroactive peptides (conotoxins) containing Gla residues, which are highly toxic. Function in Bacteria Many bacteria, such as Escherichia coli in the large intestine, synthesize vitamin K2 (menaquinone) but not vitamin K1 (phylloquinone). Menaquinone facilitates anaerobic respiration by transferring electrons between molecules. For example, an electron donor like lactate or NADH transfers electrons to menaquinone, which then transfers them to an oxidant like fumarate or nitrate. This process generates ATP, similar to eukaryotic aerobic respiration, except the final electron acceptor is not oxygen but fumarate or nitrate. E. coli can perform both aerobic respiration and menaquinone-mediated anaerobic respiration.
